tour.title: Pick a chapter
tour.text: Each tab is a region, with an overview of the chokepoints and shockwaves in it. Once a region is open, a second row lists everything inside it, one chapter each.

tour.title: Read the map
tour.text: Dark gates are chokepoints, red rings are shockwaves. Open a region and its places light up; open one place and the map shows only that place. Drag to pan, use + and − to zoom.

tour.title: Open a chokepoint or shockwave
tour.text: Every marker is also a chapter. Hover it for its name, select it to read the analysis. Some chapters add a “View data” button that puts extra layers on the map.

overview.h: An ocean of lanes and cables
p: Since the end of the Second World War, the Atlantic has been a source of security and prosperity. The ocean is key to Europe’s strategic depth and an essential component of its global connectivity. European defence has rested for decades on the Atlantic resupply chain, through which the US and Canada would send soldiers and equipment to support European NATO allies in case of an attack. The Atlantic is also Europe’s most important digital artery: key data cables pass on the Atlantic seabed, connecting Europe to North America, and increasingly to South America and West Africa. Increasingly, Europe’s energy mix is reliant on imports of LNG from the other side of the Atlantic.

Five of the EU’s top 20 trade partners in 2025 are in the Atlantic basin. [[1]] The value of EU-US trade in goods and services in 2025 was USD 2.3 trillion, showing strength despite the new tariffs. [[2]] Commercial ties with partners across the Americas (like Canada, Mexico, Brazil) and on the West coast of Africa (Morocco, Nigeria, South Africa) are also significant. These numbers are likely to rise because of recently signed trade deals with Mercosur and Mexico. [[3]] [[4]] Furthermore, trade between the EU and the West Coast of the Americas passes through the Panama Canal, making the latter a strategic chokepoint for Europe.

In addition to a long Atlantic coastline, seven EU outermost regions and nine Overseas Countries and Territories are scattered across the Atlantic basin, including strategic islands such as the Azores and Greenland, and a space launch base in French Guyana. [[5]] [[6]]
The Atlantic has long been regarded as a basin of stability for Europe. However, several threats could disrupt the ocean and affect European security.

Attacks on critical infrastructure and shipping lanes: Traditionally, this has been envisaged as Russian submarines entering the North Atlantic through the GIUK-Norway Gap and attacking military convoys, but the threat is evolving. Non-military vessels could carry out sabotage activities, including subsea cable damage or harassing activities, disrupting either commercial goods or military reinforcements.

Transnational organised criminal groups: A fluid criminal ecosystem between groups operating off the Caribbean, South American and West African coasts has emerged. They use Atlantic routes for illicit trade and drug smuggling from South America and the Caribbean to Europe, either directly or via West Africa. Some of these have established alliances on the European shore – examples include ‘Ndrangheta (Italy) and PCC (Brazil), Los Choneros (Ecuador) and Balkan groups and Mexican cartels (Sinaloa, CJNG) with EU-based networks. [[7]] These non-state groups benefit from the conditions that hostile states seek to create to Europe, such as weak governance, societal divisions, lack of interstate cooperation. This highlights the nexus between internal and external security threats in Europe and other regions.

Connections with other theatres: Crises from other theatres and chokepoints could affect the Atlantic. On the one hand, the Atlantic Ocean is a potential alternative to other trade routes. In case of disruptions in the Red Sea, goods from the Indo-Pacific can reach Europe via the South Atlantic, as was the case during the Houthi attacks in 2024. [[8]] The Panama Canal could also be an alternative for goods travelling from the Indo-Pacific to Europe, should the Strait of Malacca become unavailable.

But other theatres could also put strain on the Atlantic. The disputed waters and territories of the Arctic (from the Svalbard archipelago to Greenland) can cause spillovers into the North Atlantic. In case of a US-China confrontation, traffic along the Panama Canal could be affected. Chinese-operated ports in Latin America, the Caribbean and Africa could be used to block products or restrict maritime traffic. A crisis in the Indo-Pacific could reduce the availability of US assets for Europe, reducing the credibility of the transatlantic defence resupply chain is at the basis of NATO’s force surge in collective defence contingency. Political or trade tensions could also have a similar effect, making contributions to NATO conditional on political concessions.

This number of threats – some potential, some already existing – has significant implications for the EU. The subsections will analyse each threat more in detail and provide specific recommendations. However, when looking at the Atlantic as a whole, the EU should:

Apply a security lens to the region: the current Atlantic Strategy emphasises the blue economy, connectivity and research. [[9]] The next Macro-regional Strategy for the Atlantic, expected by June 2027, should put security at the centre. [[10]] It should also connect the Atlantic to other regions and run scenario exercises to understand the impact of external crises on the Atlantic basin.

Expand defence initiatives to the North Atlantic, focusing on securing corridors to ensure a safe passage of transatlantic defence supplies, complementing NATO activities, supporting Member States in patrolling supply corridors, protecting ports and critical infrastructure.

Connect threats and stakeholders: on the one hand, the EU should recognise the links between external and internal threats (e.g. between strategic competition and organised crime); on the other, it should cooperation with traditional defence partners (US, Canada, UK, Norway) with new security partnerships such as with Mexico, Brazil, Colombia and other Atlantic countries. Additionally, the EU could enhance cooperation and interaction between specialised agencies (military, coast guard, customs, police, intelligence) between different states, as well as between them and private critical infrastructure operators.

stake: NATO uses the acronym GIUK-NOR Gap for the naval chokepoints in the northern Atlantic Ocean between the landmasses of Greenland, Iceland, the United Kingdom and Norway. These chokepoints are the principal waterway for Russian vessels to enter the North Atlantic from its Arctic ports (see Arctic section). During the Cold War, NATO identified the Gap as the best point to track and stop Soviet submarines. In recent years, Russian activities across the Gap have increased. Between 2024 and 2025, the UK monitored a 30% increase in Russian vessels reaching its waters from the Norwegian Sea. [[1]] In April 2026, the UK Ministry of Defence exposed a covert Russian submarine operation, which could have resulted in a sabotage to critical undersea infrastructure. [[2]]

bites: The EU’s interests in these waterways are significant. Greenland, part of the Kingdom of Denmark and an EU Overseas Territory, represents the northern end of the Gap. Other Danish territories such as the Faroe Islands (not part of the EU) sit in the Gap. Even without entering the North Atlantic, hostile actors could also go down from the Norwegian into the North Sea, threatening EU Member States’ coastlines as well as key energy and telecommunications infrastructure (see the Arctic section of this project). Finally, several undersea cables travel across the North Sea and cross the GIUK Gap on their way to Iceland, Canada and the US.
prepare: Given its high interests, the EU could play a more active role in securing the GIUK-Norway Gap. NATO carries out surveillance of the waterways through patrols and sensors. However, changing maritime conditions could make this detection harder. Increased maritime traffic and warming waters defect or reduce noise propagation, making submarine detection in the North Atlantic area harder. [[3]] The EU could support this effort by promoting the production of sensors and unmanned systems to increase surveillance activities, as well as the related ISR and command-and-control platforms. Two recently agreed European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCIs) – on drone and counter-drone systems, and on integrated maritime and seabed defence – could be particularly helpful to this effort. [[4]] The EU should ensure that they are sufficiently funded to be appealing to Member States, as well as open to partners where possible and interoperable with NATO.
partners: Partners who are particularly important to the security of the GIUK-Norway gap include NATO allies Norway, the UK (who signed a new cooperation agreement for protecting the North Atlantic in 2025), Iceland, as well as Canada and the US. [[5]] The security of this region should also be connected to those of adjacent basins – both the Arctic and the North Atlantic (see relevant sections).

stake: The Panama Canal is a crucial waterway for global commerce. The most important commodities traded through the Canal include energy (oil and LNG), grains (soybeans, corn), chemicals, ores and metals, and fertilisers. This waterway is also relevant for Europe.

Between 2020 and 2023, 125,278 long tonnes of cargo coming from or destined to European ports passed through the Canal. [[1]] This route is mostly used for trade between Europe and the Americas, as well as for a small portion of trade between Europe and Asia-Oceania. As of 2023, the Europe-West Coast of South America route was the fourth most common route of cargo ships passing through the Canal. It is also important for the passage of some strategic materials such as copper, lithium and zinc, amounting to about one third of the EU’s total trade with Chile and Peru.
{{chart:panama_tonnage}}
risks: While the Canal is not the most important chokepoint for Europe, its relevance could increase in the event of geopolitical tensions elsewhere. Should the Strait of Malacca be unavailable, cargo flowing out of Asia could be redirected eastwards, crossing the Canal to reach Europe via the Atlantic. For these reasons, Europe should pay close attention to what happens in Panama.
bites: The Panama Canal has become a hotspot of geopolitical competition between the US and China. [[2]] Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison Holdings operated the Balboa and Cristóbal terminals at the Pacific and Atlantic entrances to the canal since 1997. In 2025, the US pressured Panama to change the status quo. [[3]] Panama exited China’s Belt and Road initiative, and subsequently signed an agreement to expand Washington’s military presence in the country. [[4]] In 2026, the Panamanian Supreme Court declared CK Hutchison’s port concession unconstitutional, ruling that they infringed on national sovereignty and causing irritation in Beijing. [[5]]
{{data:atl_ports|View data: Chinese-linked ports}}

Tensions between the US and China could result in a future blockade of the Canal. Global supply chain disruptions could impact energy flows, food security (due to loss of grains and fertilisers), as well as strategic sectors like chemicals (methanol, ammonium compounds and benzene) or minerals (copper, zinc, aluminium, lithium). These would impact manufacturing of products in the Americas which would eventually come to Europe, or directly impact European production.

An example of these disruptions has taken place in 2026 due to meteorological events. The Panama Canal is particularly vulnerable to climate change. According to the UN, during the low-rain season caused by El Niño in 2024, traffic along the Canal reduced by 35% due to low water levels, costing the Canal over $500 million in lost revenue. [[6]] With a new El Niño developing in 2026, a similar traffic reduction could take place. [[7]]

In addition to commerce, the Canal also contributes to international drug trade. While the bulk of cocaine to Europe depart from the Caribbean and Atlantic coast, another route crosses into the Panama Canal from the Pacific ports in Colombia, Ecuador or Peru, and then enters the Caribbean Sea. [[8]]
prepare: The EU should not see the Canal in isolation, but link it to maritime security in the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific, as well as to European security more generally. On the one hand, it blocking should tensions rise between the US and China, it may be more difficult to ensure safe passage of commercial vessels in the vicinity of the Canal, blocking a key artery for European commerce. At the same time, the Canal could also be used by hostile actors to Europe (for example, Russian-linked vessels could pass through it). Therefore, there could be situations in which locking the canal could be beneficial.
partners: The EU should map out potential ways in which the Panama Canal could be used, when it could be closed, and what positions the Union should take on the issue. As a general rule, the EU should support efforts to keep the Panama Canal open, in line with the 1977 Treaty on the Permanent Neutrality and Operation of the Panama Canal. [[9]] But the caveat above indicates that the EU could pressure for closure of the Canal to specific vessels. The EU should maintain close ties with Panama and other relevant actors in the region to deal with these contingencies.

At the same time, the EU should work reduce the transit of drugs and illicit goods through the Panama Canal towards Europe, with countries on the Western coast of the Americas (in particular, Mexico, Ecuador, Peru, Chile and Colombia) – see the examples in the Caribbean section.

stake: The North Atlantic is the highway of Europe’s biggest bilateral trade relationship. [[1]] The US, Mexico and Canada are the first, third and fourth largest EU trade partner in the Americas. The Atlantic is also Europe’s most important digital artery: 16 transatlantic data cables pass on the Atlantic seabed, connecting Europe to North America, and six more are expected to come online between 2026 and 2029. Increasingly, Europe’s energy mix is reliant on imports of LNG from the other side of the Atlantic.

European defence has rested for decades on the North Atlantic resupply chain, through which the US and Canada would send soldiers and equipment to support European NATO allies in case of an attack. Even today, NATO’s Force Model relies on the surge of weapons and personnel from US to European ports, coordinated by Joint Force Command (JFC) Norfolk in Virginia. [[2]] [[3]] Should the US withdraw further elements of its military presence in Europe, transatlantic reinforcements would become even more important in the event of a military contingency.
risks: The most direct threat to the North Atlantic would take the form of operations by hostile actors aimed at disrupting the transatlantic trade and defence resupply lanes – similar to operations carried out during the two World Wars. Russian submarines could enter the North Atlantic through the GIUK Gap. [[4]] Long-range anti-ship and anti-air systems onboard these submarines could enable Russia to create A2/AD zones in the North Atlantic, where NATO planes and ships cannot operate without fear of being shot down or sunk. [[5]]

Russia might not limit its set of tools to submarines or military vessels. Taking a page from its hybrid playbook in the Baltic Sea, Russian commercial or research ships could carry out sabotage activities in the North Atlantic, entering either from the GIUK Gap, the Baltic and North Sea, or the Mediterranean. These vessels could carry uncrewed underwater systems (developed by GUGI, the Russian Navy’s deep-sea research unit) which could target critical undersea infrastructure. [[6]] The sheer size of the area to protect makes it harder to prevent this type of threat. Russia could also use drones from the ships to harass convoys in the Atlantic.
bites: These are not the only ways in which transatlantic defence and trade could be disrupted. A crisis in other theatres (such as the Western Hemisphere or the Indo-Pacific) could reduce the availability of US assets in the Atlantic. The current shortages of US air defence interceptors in Europe due to the war in Iran are an example of what could happen in the future. Political tensions in the US-Europe relationship, during the Trump administration or in future ones, could also disrupt trade and reduce the credibility of the defence resupply chain. These risks are not limited to goods and services coming into Europe, but also to European outward investments. For instance, in the wake of the new US tariffs, 73% of EU companies operating in the US claim to have experienced negative impacts on their business, including eroding competitiveness, raising costs, and loss of costumers. [[7]] Further political uncertainty could impacting decisions to invest in the US, making the transatlantic economy weaker. [[8]]
prepare: The EU’s priorities for the North Atlantic should focus on ensuring the safety of transatlantic trade and defence connections, protecting key infrastructure, and supporting military contingencies. The EU could play a role in securing corridors to ensure a safe passage of transatlantic supply routes, while also protecting critical infrastructure. While NATO’s JFC Norfolk will likely take the lead, the EU can focus on non-NATO Member States such as Ireland and its territorial waters, using Art 42.7 contingencies if needed). The protection of military convoys as they approach the European continent could be added to the military mobility package and to the Connecting Europe Facility. [[9]] [[10]]
partners: The EU should continue to maintain positive ties with Washington where possible, even if new political tensions emerge. The EU and Member States should emphasise the importance of EU-US trade for the US economy, and on Washington’s interest in ensuring that threats from other seas do not reach the Atlantic, from where they could target the US mainland. The (apparent) resolution of the Greenland dispute may provide new momentum for practical cooperation in the North Atlantic. [[11]] Nevertheless, Europe should not be naïve about the diminishing US ability and willingness to supply Europe in a crisis. In the case of a smaller American surge, Europe must also focus on ensuring reinforcements from Canada. EU-Canada maritime security cooperation, including protection of underwater cables and security of supply routes, could be a particularly fruitful complement to existing NATO frameworks. Mexico could also be a helpful partner: albeit not a NATO ally, the country is deeply integrated in the North American economy and in transatlantic trade.

Given the sheer size of the Atlantic, monitoring threats is much harder than in a shallow, closed sea like the Baltic. The EU should support the development and production of unmanned systems at scale to ensure persistent surveillance – both at surface level and underwater. Closer cooperation with companies owning the physical infrastructure and partner countries would also be important.

stake: The Caribbean Sea and Central Atlantic may seem peripheral to European interests compared to other regions. However, the EU has direct and indirect interests in the basin and the adjacent waters. Six EU Overseas Countries and as well as four Outermost Regions are in the Caribbean Basin and South America. In the northern coast of South America, French Guyana hosts Europe's Spaceport, the ESA base whose proximity to the equator makes it ideal to launch spacecraft into a near-equatorial, geostationary orbit compared to other launch sites at higher latitudes in Europe. [[1]] Two transatlantic data cables, Atlantis 2 and EllaLink, connect Europe to the South American coast (with Atlantic2 also connecting to West Africa). [[2]]
risks: Latin America is home to some of the world’s most capable transnational criminal organisations, including the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation Cartels (in Mexico), Can del Golf and ELN (Colombia), PCC and Comando Vermelho (Brazil). [[3]] The Caribbean and Central Atlantic region is one of the main routes for narcotraffic towards Europe. [[4]] Colombia, Bolivia and Peru together grew 99.5% of global cocaine in 2020, with Europe consuming 21 percent of global demand. [[5]] [[6]] Many transnational criminal organisations smuggle cocaine and other illicit substances coming from Central America (from Mexico) and South America (from Colombia and the Andean region) to European ports – especially Antwerp, Rotterdam, Hamburg, Le Havre and Algeciras. [[7]] [[8]] The main route departs from northeastern South American ports, sometimes stopping off West Africa, including on EU territories like the Canaries and Madeira, or via ‘island hopping’ (moving drugs from island to island, typically in go-fast boats) in the Caribbean. [[5]] [[9]]

Instability and the encroachment of hostile actors in the region is another source of insecurity. Countries like China, Russia and Iran (through Hezbollah) have established a presence in the region thanks to contact with authoritarian regimes in Cuba, Venezuela and Nicaragua. [[10]] Recent events – such as the removal of Maduro from Venezuela, the ongoing US pressure campaign over Cuba, and the degradation of Hezbollah in the Middle East - have dealt a blow to these countries’ alliances in the region. [[11]]

Nevertheless, their presence has not been eradicated. China’s footprint in the Caribbean and Central Atlantic remains strong, thanks to massive investments in infrastructure. According to CSIS, Chinese companies finance, build or directly operate 37 port facilities in Latin America, 25 of which are in the Caribbean and Atlantic coastlines. [[12]] These include Russia, meanwhile, remains relevant in the region via the information space, thanks to RT and Sputnik in the Spanish-speaking world. [[13]] Their activities have the potential of disrupting EU trade (for instance, by blocking port operations or stoking anti-European sentiment in the context of a crisis) and cooperation to tackle countering transatlantic drug flows.
bites: Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, the US has become increasingly active in the Americas. According to the Pentagon, the Caribbean and the northern coast of South America are part of the Greater North America, the new perimeter of homeland defence. [[14]] Since September 2025, the US has been carrying out military strikes on suspected narcotrafficking boats across the Caribbean basin. [[15]] It has also set up partnerships with military forces across the region – especially with politically aligned governments – to counter narcotrafficking, bringing them together in the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (ACCC, also known as “Shield of the Americas”). [[16]]

While these activities have disrupted narcotrafficking routes, the emphasis on military measures risks repeating past errors in counternarcotics operations, such as ignoring non-military means like police training and local capacity building. At the same time, the military strikes may not be weakening organised groups, but simply forcing them to adapt and displacing smuggling routes away from the Caribbean and towards the Atlantic, therefore contributing to further flows to Europe. [[17]]

Other forms of instability in the region could also impact Europe. Cuba is now the subject of new US economic pressure. Having lost Venezuela as main ally and energy partner, and under disastrous domestic economic situation, the Cuban regime is in dire straits. The transition that the US engineered in Venezuela could be more difficult to replicate in Cuba, because there the economic model run by the Castro family and the GAESA military conglomerate is too entrenched in the Cuban system to allow for a transition. A major humanitarian or political crisis could trigger refugee waves that could also reach Europe.
prepare: The EU’s priority should be curbing the flow of illicit drugs across the Atlantic, while ensuring maritime security that enables the expected expansion of trade flows with the region (as a result of the updated EU-Mexico Global Agreement and the EU-Mercosur Trade Agreement).

The EU should position itself as a complement rather than a rival to US-led, military-heavy counter-narcotic efforts. Several EU-led projects (such as CRIMJUST III, SEACOP VI, El PACTO 2.0, and AIRCOP VI) focus on strengthening cooperation against organised crime with Latin American and Caribbean countries. [[18]] The EU should double down on efforts to strengthen capacity building among law enforcement authorities in the region. Specific emphasis should be placed on intelligence sharing – for instance, by replicating the European-Ecuadorian Fusion Centre in the Caribbean – and on the adoption of dual-use technologies such as drones to monitor, locate and disrupt criminal activities. [[19]]
